cards.text: The apostle John, one of Jesus' twelve disciples, is writing to believers he calls beloved, and he just told them God has given them His Spirit. Now he warns them: don't believe every spirit. Baker, that's my rule for every text that says I won a FREE cruise.

cards.question: John tells his beloved readers not to believe every spirit. What should they do instead?

answers.text: Test them to see if they're from God
Stay far away from every spirit
Trust the one that sounds the kindest

cards.question: Why do John's readers need to test the spirits? Because many false ___ have gone out into the world.

cards.text: I test every batch with one bite, okay FOUR bites, but John's test for a spirit is simpler. It all comes down to what that spirit says about Jesus.

cards.question: John's test: a spirit from God confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. That means Jesus came as a real ___.
John says a spirit that does not confess Jesus can still be from God.

cards.text: John even gives that spirit a name. It's the spirit of the antichrist, and his readers had already heard it was coming.

cards.question: John's readers had heard the spirit of the antichrist was coming. When does John say it shows up in the world?

answers.text: It comes at the very end

cards.text: False prophets out there AND that spirit already here? Friend, I'd be diving back under the takeout menus in my old junk drawer. But John's got good news for his readers.

cards.question: John calls his readers little children and tells them they're from God and have overcome. What reason does he give?

answers.text: Someone greater is in them than in the world
They far outnumber the false prophets in the world
They were taught better than the false prophets

cards.text: Then John turns back to the false prophets. He says they are of the world.

cards.question: Since these false prophets are of the world, how do they speak?
John says the world refuses to listen to the false prophets.

cards.text: Of COURSE the world listens. That's like asking your own group chat if your idea is good. Then John says, "We are from God."

cards.question: John says some people listen to "us" and some don't. Who does he say listens?
John says who listens and who doesn't is how we know the Spirit of ___ and the spirit of ___.

findings.problem: Card 1 says the letter is from 'The apostle John, one of Jesus' twelve disciples.' 1 John never names its author. The cited verses (1 John 3:24-4:1) don't support it, and no other verse does. Authorship of 1 John is a church tradition, not a stated Bible fact.
findings.question: The docs allow 'who wrote a letter, with their reference,' and 'every Bible fact he states carries its reference.' How should Papa Dorin name the author of a letter that doesn't name its writer, like 1 John, Hebrews or James's traditional identity? Should he say 'the apostle John' as fact, mark it as tradition ('the letter traditionally credited to John'), or name no author?

findings.problem: This story card is 3 sentences: 'False prophets out there AND that spirit already here?' / 'Friend, I'd be diving back under the takeout menus in my old junk drawer.' / 'But John's got good news for his readers.' Only the opening card can be up to 3 sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card uses the false prophets from 1 John 4:1, but it cites 1 John 4:3-4. Its opening line also looks back at what was already told (false prophets, the spirit already here) instead of moving the passage forward.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: This story card is 3 sentences: 'Of COURSE the world listens.' / 'That's like asking your own group chat if your idea is good.' / 'Then John says, "We are from God."'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'It comes at the very end' could be argued as right. 1 John 4:3 itself says the readers 'have heard is coming,' and card 7 just told the baker it was coming. A baker could reasonably defend this pick.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.
